ENERGY-BASED MODELS · PAPER NOTESNOV 2026

An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning

Bo DaiBased on joint work with Yilun DuNovember 2026~7 min read
CONTENTS—TL;DR01Three choices02Inference: sampling and optimization03Learning has one gradient04A map of existing methods05New algorithms by replacing one component06Limitations
Energy · inference · learning

TL;DR

An energy-based model (EBM) defines a distribution through a scalar energy, pθ(x)∝exp⁡(−Eθ(x))p_\theta(x) \propto \exp(-E_\theta(x))pθ​(x)∝exp(−Eθ​(x)). Any EBM is specified by three choices: the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. Discriminative models, generative models, representation learning, reinforcement learning and planning, and inference-time computation are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This post summarizes our tutorial, An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning ↗, with Yilun Du, which grew out of my course CSE 6243 at Georgia Tech.

// § 01

Three choices

An EBM defines the density

pθ(x)=exp⁡(−Eθ(x))Zθ,Zθ=∫exp⁡(−Eθ(x)) dx.p_\theta(x) = \frac{\exp(-E_\theta(x))}{Z_\theta}, \qquad Z_\theta = \int \exp(-E_\theta(x))\,dx.pθ​(x)=Zθ​exp(−Eθ​(x))​,Zθ​=∫exp(−Eθ​(x))dx.

We focus on the probabilistic form, as the tutorial does. EBMs can also be non-probabilistic (LeCun et al. 2006 ↗): the energy only scores compatibility, inference is minimization, and no partition function is needed. This is the zero-temperature limit of the probabilistic view (§02), and learning then uses margin or regularized losses instead of likelihood.

Low energy means a plausible configuration. The partition function ZθZ_\thetaZθ​ is usually intractable, and almost every difficulty with EBMs comes from it.

The same energy with different partition functions gives different distributions. For an energy Eθ(x,y)E_\theta(x, y)Eθ​(x,y), the joint and the conditional are

pθ(x,y)=exp⁡(−Eθ(x,y))Zθ,Zθ=∬exp⁡(−Eθ(x,y)) dx dy,pθ(y∣x)=exp⁡(−Eθ(x,y))Zθ(x),Zθ(x)=∫exp⁡(−Eθ(x,y)) dy.\begin{aligned} p_\theta(x, y) &= \frac{\exp(-E_\theta(x, y))}{Z_\theta}, & Z_\theta &= \iint \exp(-E_\theta(x, y))\,dx\,dy, \\ p_\theta(y \mid x) &= \frac{\exp(-E_\theta(x, y))}{Z_\theta(x)}, & Z_\theta(x) &= \int \exp(-E_\theta(x, y))\,dy. \end{aligned}pθ​(x,y)pθ​(y∣x)​=Zθ​exp(−Eθ​(x,y))​,=Zθ​(x)exp(−Eθ​(x,y))​,​Zθ​Zθ​(x)​=∬exp(−Eθ​(x,y))dxdy,=∫exp(−Eθ​(x,y))dy.​

Many classic models are EBMs with a particular energy. The exponential family exp⁡(θ⊤f(x))/Zθ\exp(\theta^\top f(x))/Z_\thetaexp(θ⊤f(x))/Zθ​ has an energy linear in θ\thetaθ; it is also the maximum entropy model under moment constraints on fff. Markov and conditional random fields sum log-potentials over cliques. The restricted Boltzmann machine has a bilinear energy −x⊤Ay-x^\top A y−x⊤Ay plus biases.

Once the energy is fixed, two questions remain: how to draw samples from it or find its minimum (inference), and how to fit it to data (learning). These three choices organize the rest of the post.

// § 02

Inference: sampling and optimization

An EBM gives an unnormalized density, so inference needs a procedure. There are three families. MCMC, such as Langevin dynamics, follows −∇xEθ(x)-\nabla_x E_\theta(x)−∇x​Eθ​(x) plus noise and needs no partition function. Variational inference fits a tractable distribution to pθp_\thetapθ​. Amortized samplers train a network that maps noise to samples in one pass. Taking the zero-temperature limit turns sampling into optimization, arg⁡min⁡xEθ(x)\arg\min_x E_\theta(x)argminx​Eθ​(x).

The same three families appear whether the samples are images, tokens, or actions. The trade-off is also the same: an iterative sampler pays at every input but adapts to a new energy immediately, while an amortized sampler pays once during training and then needs one forward pass.

// § 03

Learning has one gradient

The learning methods for EBMs look different: maximum likelihood, contrastive divergence, pseudolikelihood, score matching, noise-contrastive estimation, and adversarial training. Their gradients share one structure. Each lowers the energy of the data and raises the energy of a set of negative samples drawn from some sampler qqq:

∇θL(θ)=Ex∼pd[∇θEθ(x)]−Ex∼q[∇θEθ(x)].\nabla_\theta L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_d}\big[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x)\big] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q}\big[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x)\big].∇θ​L(θ)=Ex∼pd​​[∇θ​Eθ​(x)]−Ex∼q​[∇θ​Eθ​(x)].

Maximum likelihood is the case q=pθq = p_\thetaq=pθ​. The other methods replace pθp_\thetapθ​ with a qqq that is cheaper to draw from, and they differ mainly in this choice.

MethodNegative sampler qqqGap from pθp_\thetapθ​
Maximum likelihoodpθp_\thetapθ​none
Contrastive divergencekkk MCMC steps from datashort chains
Pseudolikelihoodone Gibbs step from dataone variable at a time
Score matchingone small Langevin step from datalocal
NCEreweighted data and noiseexact only at the optimum
Adversarial traininga learned samplerhow well it tracks pθp_\thetapθ​

The view also tells where each method loses accuracy: wherever qqq differs from pθp_\thetapθ​, the gradient differs from the maximum likelihood gradient. Contrastive divergence and score matching start at the data and move a short distance, so they never visit a spurious low-energy region far from the data, and never correct it.

// § 04

A map of existing methods

Many methods developed separately, under different names and motivations, are EBMs with particular choices of the three components. They differ less in what they model than in how they handle the partition function and sampling, which leads to different parametrizations that hide the underlying EBM. The table lists a few representative methods in each area.

AreaMethodsAs an EBM
Discriminativelogistic regression, CRFs, SPENsconditional EBMs that differ in the structure of the energy over outputs
GenerativeGANsa potential paired with a learned sampler
normalizing flows, autoregressive modelsenergies restricted so that ZθZ_\thetaZθ​ is tractable and sampling takes one pass
diffusion and flow modelslearn the score of noise-perturbed EBMs
RepresentationSimCLR, CLIP, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encodersone bilinear EBM whose factors are the representation, fit by different learning methods
Decision makingmaximum-entropy RL (SBEED, soft Q-learning), KL-regularized RLHFEBM policies in closed form
inverse RL, imitation learning (GAIL, IBC)EBMs fit from demonstrations
planninginference in an EBM over trajectories
EBM world modelsan EBM over transitions whose factors make value functions linear
Inference-time computationbest-of-NNN (WIND, inference-aware fine-tuning), search, iterative refinementsamplers for one residual EBM: a generator composed with a verifier

The last row of the table is the most recent. Given a pretrained generator π0\pi_0π0​ and a verifier rrr, the target of inference-time computation is the residual EBM

π⋆(y∣x)=π0(y∣x)exp⁡(r(x,y)/λ)Z(x),\pi^\star(y \mid x) = \frac{\pi_0(y \mid x)\exp\big(r(x, y)/\lambda\big)}{Z(x)},π⋆(y∣x)=Z(x)π0​(y∣x)exp(r(x,y)/λ)​,

which is also the optimal policy of KL-regularized fine-tuning. Best-of-NNN, search, and refinement are samplers for π⋆\pi^\starπ⋆; fine-tuning amortizes the same sampler. The two differ in whether the cost is paid during training or at inference. Best-of-NNN sampling fine-tuning lies between them: it keeps best-of-NNN at inference and trains the generator for it.

// § 05

New algorithms by replacing one component

A view is useful only if it changes what we can do. The EBM view helps in two ways. First, it locates the bottleneck of a method in one component, which can then be replaced while the others are kept:

  • Representation. Contrastive learning such as CLIP fits the bilinear EBM by NCE, whose quality depends on the batch size. Fitting the same EBM by maximum likelihood with an amortized partition function removes this dependence (AmorLIP); fitting it by score matching gives diffusion spectral representations.
  • Diffusion policies. In online RL, the target policy is known only through its energy, so denoising score matching has no samples to train on. Reweighting the score matching loss makes it trainable on samples from the current policy (diffusion policy optimization).
  • Exploration. The log-partition function of an EBM policy is an optimistic estimate of the value, so using it as a regularizer gives optimism for exploration and pessimism for offline learning, without explicit uncertainty estimates (VAC, VPO).

Second, it gives a capability that other views lack: composition. Energies of independently trained models can be combined at inference time, without retraining:

  • AND: add the energies, EA+EBE_A + E_BEA​+EB​, a product of distributions.
  • OR: the soft minimum, −log⁡(e−EA+e−EB)-\log\big(e^{-E_A} + e^{-E_B}\big)−log(e−EA​+e−EB​), a mixture.
  • NOT: subtract an energy, EB−EA+CE_B - E_A + CEB​−EA​+C.

Classifier-free guidance is already such a composition: an inversion that divides the conditional model by a power of the unconditional one. In planning, learned dynamics, behavior priors, goals, and constraints each contribute an energy term, and a new task is a new sum of terms.

// § 06

Limitations

The EBM view explains how methods relate and suggests which component to change, but it does not predict how well the result will work. Two methods that fit the same energy with the same learning method can still behave very differently, depending on the parametrization, the architecture, the data augmentations, and the optimization. The view gives coarse guidance, such as maximum likelihood for calibrated likelihoods, score matching for sampling, and NCE for relative scores, but the choice among them is still empirical. Composition is meaningful only when the component energies have compatible scales and the product is normalizable, and the composed landscape can be much harder to sample than each component.

The full version, with derivations and a table placing every method on the three components, is on arXiv ↗.
